guides.title: The universal pattern (read this first)
guides.tagline: Every third-party service sets up the same way
guides.intro: Stripe, Resend, OpenAI, Twilio — they all follow one shape. Learn it once and every new service is a variation, not a mystery.
steps: 1. Create an account on the provider's site — use a login you control long-term (work email, not a throwaway)
2. Find the API keys page — there are almost always TWO keys: test/sandbox and live/production
3. Put the TEST key in your local env vars — build the whole feature against test mode
4. Add the key to Render → Environment — never in code, never committed
5. If the service calls YOU back (payment succeeded, email delivered), that's a webhook — you build an endpoint, give them the URL, and verify their signing secret
6. Test the failure path — what does your app do when the API is down or the key is wrong? (It should degrade, not crash)
7. Only when it all works: swap to LIVE keys in production env vars, test keys stay for dev
traps: Test vs live keys mixed up — the #1 integration bug. Your dev runs on test keys forever; live keys only ever live in production env vars.
Webhook secrets skipped — without verifying the signature, anyone can POST fake 'payment succeeded' events to your endpoint.
No fallback — when the provider has an outage (they all do), your app should degrade gracefully, not hang.

guides.title: Email — Resend, SendGrid, Amazon SES
guides.tagline: Sending real email that lands in inboxes, not spam
guides.intro: You cannot reliably send email from your own server — it goes straight to spam. You need an email service. Resend is the friendliest for small apps; SES is cheapest at volume but more complex.
steps: Pick a provider — Resend is the novice-friendly default (free tier ~100 emails/day, clean API, one API key)
Verify your domain (resend.com → Domains → add the DNS records they show you in your registrar). Until verified you can only send to yourself — that's normal, it's anti-spam
API key → env var (RESEND_API_KEY). Send test emails to yourself first
Build the send path behind ONE function — every feature calls send_email(), never the API directly. That one place is where you add logging, sandboxing, and fallback
Sandbox first — add a mode that blocks real sends to non-test addresses. A test script accidentally emailing 500 real users is a real-world trap that actually happens
traps: Sending from an unverified domain — instant spam folder or outright rejection.
No sandbox — one stray test script emails your entire user base. The CRM built its sandbox after exactly this near-miss.
Secrets in the from-address logic — 'from' must be a domain you verified, not a customer's email.

guides.title: Payments — Stripe
guides.tagline: Taking money without touching card numbers
guides.intro: Never handle card numbers yourself — that's a compliance nightmare (PCI). Stripe Checkout or Payment Links host the card form; you just get told 'paid' via webhook.
steps: Create a Stripe account → get the TEST keys (pk_test_… and sk_test_…) from the dashboard
Decide the product shape first: one-off payment, subscription, or credits top-up — they're different Stripe objects
Use Stripe Checkout (hosted page) or Payment Links — the card form lives on Stripe's servers, which is what keeps you out of PCI scope
Build the webhook endpoint — the payment 'succeeded' event arrives there. Verify the webhook signing secret (whsec_…) or anyone can fake a payment
Record payments in your own DB as ledger rows keyed to Stripe IDs — Stripe is the money rail, YOUR database is the source of truth for what a user is owed
Test the full loop with Stripe's test cards (4242 4242 4242 4242) including failure cards — then flip to live keys
traps: Trusting the browser redirect instead of the webhook — users close tabs; the webhook is the authoritative 'paid' signal.
Skipping signature verification on webhooks — forged 'payment succeeded' events are a real attack.
Double-charging on retries — subscriptions and renewals need idempotent handling; the CRM's cancelled-subscription incident is exactly this class of bug.

guides.title: AI providers — Gemini, Anthropic, OpenAI
guides.tagline: Adding AI features without burning money
guides.intro: Each provider has a console where you create an API key. Gemini has a real free tier (aistudio.google.com — no card); Anthropic and OpenAI are prepaid but cheap for small apps.
steps: Start with Gemini's free tier to validate the feature — upgrade to a paid provider when usage or quality demands it
Write your calls behind one wrapper function (call_ai(system, history)) with a provider switch — so you can swap providers by changing an env var, not rewriting code
Meter every call — AI costs money per request. Log usage per user and cap it (credits, rate limits) or a bot will run up your bill
Set max_tokens and timeouts on every call — an uncapped response or a hung request is a silent cost/hang
Design the offline fallback — when the provider is down or the user is out of credits, the app should still do something useful
traps: No metering — AI is the one integration where a bored user or bot can cost you real money per request.
Silent failures — log provider errors; a fallback that swallows errors means you never know the AI is broken (happened in this very build).
User secrets in prompts — warn users not to paste API keys/passwords into AI chats; providers log them.

guides.title: Social login — Google, GitHub OAuth
guides.tagline: 'Sign in with Google' so users skip passwords
guides.intro: OAuth lets users log in with an existing account. You register your app with the provider, they send the user back with proof of identity. Removes password-reset support burden too.
steps: Register your app at the provider's console (Google Cloud Console / GitHub Developer Settings) — you get a client ID + secret
Set the redirect URL exactly — providers reject mismatches; you'll need one for localhost AND one for production
The flow: your button → provider's consent page → back to your callback URL with a code → your backend exchanges the code for the user's verified email
Link by email — if they signed up with password then use Google with the same email, connect the accounts (or reject clearly)
Client secret goes in env vars; the client ID is public and fine in frontend code
traps: Redirect URI mismatch — the most common OAuth error; every environment needs its URL registered.
Trusting the frontend's copy of the identity — always verify the code exchange server-side.
Assuming emails are verified — only some providers guarantee it; check the verified flag.

guides.title: Error tracking — Sentry
guides.tagline: Know it broke before users tell you
guides.intro: When your app crashes for a user, you shouldn't find out via email. Sentry captures errors with stack traces, context, and counts — free tier covers small apps.
steps: Create a Sentry project → get a DSN (it's a public key, safe to ship in frontend code)
Backend: one SDK init line captures unhandled exceptions automatically
Frontend: same — React errors get reported with component context
Add user context (id/email) to events — 'which user hit this?' is the first debugging question
Set alert rules — email/Slack on new error types, not every repeat
traps: Logging passwords/tokens — scrub sensitive fields (Sentry does this by default for common names, but check).
Alert fatigue — if every trivial error pings you, you'll mute the channel and miss the real one.

guides.title: File & image storage — S3, Cloudinary
guides.tagline: User uploads don't belong in your database or repo
guides.intro: Uploaded files (avatars, PDFs, photos) go to object storage, not your app server or MongoDB. Cloudinary is friendliest for images; S3 is the standard for everything else.
steps: Create a bucket/storage account; get access keys → env vars
Upload via signed URLs — the browser uploads straight to storage; your server just signs the permission slip (keeps big files off your server)
Store only the file's URL/key in your database, never the file bytes
Set file size + type limits server-side — signed URLs don't stop a user uploading a 2GB file
Private files need signed download URLs too — a public URL pattern means anyone who guesses the name gets the file
traps: Files in the database — fine for a 10KB logo, disastrous for real uploads (Mongo docs cap at 16MB anyway).
Public buckets — check bucket policy; 'private by default' is not universal.
No malware/type check — a user uploads an .exe named photo.jpg; validate content type, not just extension.

guides.title: SMS — Twilio
guides.tagline: Text messages for codes and alerts
guides.intro: SMS needs a provider and usually a rented phone number. Twilio is the standard. SMS costs per message — meter it like AI calls.
steps: Create a Twilio account → get Account SID + Auth Token → env vars
Buy a number (or use their trial number — trial SMS only goes to verified numbers)
Rate-limit sends hard — SMS costs ~$0.01–0.08 each and 'SMS pumping' bots exist to run up bills
For verification codes: generate the code server-side, store it hashed with an expiry, never in the URL
traps: Unmetered sends — SMS pumping fraud is real; cap sends per user/IP per day.
Codes that never expire — verification codes should live minutes, not days.

guides.title: Analytics — Plausible, PostHog
guides.intro: Skip Google Analytics — heavy, cookie-banner-requiring. Plausible and PostHog are lightweight, privacy-friendly, and don't need a consent banner for basic stats.
steps: Add the provider's snippet/script to your frontend (Plausible: one script tag; PostHog: one SDK init)
Track the few events that matter — signup, project created, stage passed — not every click
Decide what you won't collect — a written line ('no keystrokes, no chat content') is a feature you can put on the security page
Use it to answer questions, not to hoard data — 'where do users drop off?' beats 'everything, just in case'
traps: Tracking personal content — mentor chats and user answers are private; analytics should see events, not content.
Dashboard wallpaper — data you never look at is a liability, not an asset.
